title: Hydraulics and fluid flow: pressure, speed and energy
voiceInstructions: Speak as a warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Sound relaxed, lovely, welcoming and lightly playful, like explaining an interesting discovery to a student beside you. Use a gentle smile in the voice, expressive but subtle changes in pitch, natural contractions and conversational rhythm. Let curiosity and small moments of delight come through without exaggerated acting, baby talk, singing or a sales pitch. Avoid a flat, robotic or overly polished announcer cadence. Keep scientific terms precise. Slow down a little for equations, decimal numbers and unit conversions; separate the factors clearly. Give a brief natural thinking pause after a question, then explain with calm confidence. Do not add words or laughter that are absent from the script.

chapters.title: A small push can support a large load
chapters.formula: F1/A1 = F2/A2 for ideal pistons at the same height
points: Pascal's principle transmits an applied pressure change through an enclosed fluid.
Assume negligible friction, piston weight and pressure losses.
Area ratio 10 with input force 50 N gives output force 500 N.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Last time we explored water at rest. Today, let's use pressure to lift a load, then follow a fluid as it moves. Picture a hydraulic lift with a small piston connected by liquid to a larger piston. Push on the small piston, and you increase the pressure of the enclosed fluid. Pascal's principle says that applied pressure change is transmitted throughout the fluid. Pressure is shared; force depends on piston area. For ideal pistons at the same height, with negligible friction and piston weight, input force divided by input area equals output force divided by output area. Suppose the output piston has ten times the area of the input piston. Push with fifty newtons. What load force can it balance? Take a moment. Ten times fifty gives five hundred newtons. That feels like a useful bargain. But a bigger force doesn't mean we've created energy. We'll check the distance moved next. If the pistons are at different heights, include the hydrostatic pressure difference. Pascal's principle concerns the transmitted pressure change; it doesn't erase the existing variation of pressure with depth.

chapters.title: The price of force multiplication is distance
chapters.formula: A1 x1 = A2 x2; ideal work: F1 x1 = F2 x2
points: An incompressible liquid transfers equal displaced volumes.
Area ratio 10: input piston travels ten times the output distance.
50 N through 0.20 m and 500 N through 0.02 m both give 10 J.
chapters.script: Let's see where the bargain comes from. Our liquid is approximately incompressible, and we're neglecting leaks. When the small piston moves down, the volume it pushes into the connecting region must equal the volume raised beneath the large piston. Piston volume is area times distance moved. So input area times input displacement equals output area times output displacement. If the large area is ten times the small area, the large piston travels only one tenth as far. Push the small piston down twenty centimetres, and the large piston rises two centimetres. Now check the work. Fifty newtons times zero point two zero metres is ten joules. Five hundred newtons times zero point zero two metres is also ten joules. Larger force, smaller distance: energy is accounted for. Real machines lose some energy through friction and other effects, so their useful output work is smaller. Here is a JEE trap to dodge. If a question doubles piston radius, its area becomes four times larger. Force multiplication depends on the area ratio, not directly on the radius ratio. Start with pi r squared before making the comparison.

chapters.title: Continuity: the same flow through each section
chapters.formula: Q = A v; for steady incompressible flow A1 v1 = A2 v2
points: v is the mean speed across the cross section.
Assume a full pipe, no leaks and no branches between sections.
Area 4 cm squared at 2 m/s gives Q = 0.0008 m cubed/s.
chapters.script: Now open a flow path and watch liquid move through a pipe. Imagine marking two cross sections. In steady flow, fluid doesn't keep accumulating between them. The mass entering each second equals the mass leaving each second. For constant density, the volume flow rate is the same at both sections. We call it capital Q, and calculate it as area times mean flow speed. This gives the continuity equation: area one times speed one equals area two times speed two. Suppose a pipe section has area four square centimetres and mean speed two metres per second. Convert the area: four square centimetres is zero point zero zero zero four square metres. The volume flow rate is zero point zero zero zero eight cubic metres per second, or zero point eight litres per second. At a section of area one square centimetre, the speed becomes eight metres per second. The liquid speeds up to pass the same volume through a smaller opening. We're assuming steady incompressible flow, a full pipe, and no leaks or branches between these sections. For changing density, conserve mass using density times area times speed instead. Continuity comes from conservation of mass, not from a pressure equation.

chapters.title: Bernoulli: account for energy along the flow
chapters.formula: p + (1/2)rho v squared + rho g y = constant along a streamline
points: Use steady, incompressible flow with negligible viscous losses.
No pump or turbine adds or removes energy between the chosen points.
Horizontal water flow changing 2 to 4 m/s gives pressure drop 6000 Pa.
chapters.script: Continuity tells us how flow speed changes. Bernoulli's equation connects that speed to pressure and height. For steady incompressible flow with negligible viscous losses, along a streamline, add three terms: pressure, one half density times speed squared, and density times g times height. Their sum stays constant when no pump or turbine adds or removes energy between the points. Think of this as an energy account per unit volume. Now take two points at the same height in an ideal water flow. Speed increases from two to four metres per second. How much does pressure decrease? The height terms cancel. The pressure drop is one half times one thousand times the difference between four squared and two squared. Sixteen minus four is twelve, giving six thousand pascals. If the first pressure is one hundred twenty thousand pascals, the second is one hundred fourteen thousand. Faster flow has lower pressure in this particular comparison. Keep the conditions attached to that conclusion: equal height, the same streamline, and the ideal assumptions. Don't automatically apply that slogan to every moving fluid. First decide whether continuity, energy conservation, or both are needed.

chapters.title: A small outlet: derive the speed instead of guessing
chapters.formula: v(outlet) = sqrt(2gh) for a large open tank and small outlet
points: Both the free surface and the emerging jet are at atmospheric pressure.
A large tank makes free-surface speed negligible compared with outlet speed.
Depth 1.25 m with g = 10 m/s squared gives ideal exit speed 5 m/s.
chapters.script: Let's finish with a tank draining through a small opening. The tank is open to the atmosphere, and the outlet is also open to air. Choose one point at the free surface and the other in the emerging jet. Their pressures are both atmospheric, so those terms cancel in Bernoulli's equation. If the tank is much wider than the outlet, continuity tells us the surface moves down much more slowly than the jet moves out. Neglect the surface speed. A vertical drop h then becomes kinetic energy per unit volume, giving outlet speed equal to the square root of two g h. With a depth of one point two five metres and g equal to ten, two g h is twenty five. The ideal exit speed is five metres per second. Pause and predict what happens when the depth becomes four times larger. The speed doubles, because of the square root. Real outlet flow can differ because of viscosity, jet contraction and other losses. As a large tank drains, we use this as a slowly changing, approximately steady model at each instant. Your checklist is pressure reference, vertical height, flow continuity and energy assumptions. Next we'll need separate ideas for viscosity and surface tension.

quiz.question: An ideal hydraulic lift at equal piston heights has output area ten times its input area. Input force 50 N balances output force:
quiz.explanation: Equal pressure increments give F2 = F1 A2/A1 = 50 x 10 = 500 N.

quiz.question: In that ideal incompressible lift, input displacement 0.20 m produces output displacement:
quiz.explanation: Equal transferred volumes give x2 = x1 A1/A2 = 0.20/10 = 0.02 m.

quiz.question: Steady incompressible flow has mean speed 2 m/s at area 4 cm squared. At area 1 cm squared, its mean speed is:
quiz.explanation: A1 v1 = A2 v2 gives v2 = 4 x 2/1 = 8 m/s.

quiz.question: Along a horizontal streamline in ideal water flow of density 1000 kg/m cubed, speed rises from 2 to 4 m/s. Pressure drops by:
quiz.explanation: Pressure drop = 0.5 x 1000 x (4 squared - 2 squared) = 6000 Pa.

quiz.question: A small outlet is 1.25 m below the surface of a large open tank. With g = 10 and ideal flow, exit speed is:
quiz.explanation: v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 1.25) = sqrt(25) = 5 m/s.
